title: Spreading facial swelling in a patient with diabetes
stem:
A 46-year-old woman attends your practice as an emergency at 4:30 pm on a Friday. She has had a toothache from her **lower right first molar** for five days, worsening despite co-codamol from the pharmacy. Since last night her face has been swelling.

Her medical history includes **type 2 diabetes** (metformin, last HbA1c "high — about 75"), and she mentions she has felt "shivery and rough" since this morning and has barely drunk anything today.

On examination she has a **firm, tender right submandibular swelling crossing the lower border of the mandible**, with early loss of definition toward the midline. **Mouth opening is limited to about 22 mm.** She is drooling slightly and says swallowing is becoming uncomfortable. The floor of the mouth on the right feels raised and firm. The lower right first molar is grossly carious and tender to percussion.

Observations taken at the practice: **temperature 38.6 °C, pulse 118, respiratory rate 21, BP 104/66.**

domains.name: Information gathering, assimilation & diagnosis
domains.model_answer:
My headline: this is a **spreading odontogenic infection with airway red flags and features of sepsis in an immunocompromised patient** — this is a medical emergency, so my assessment is rapid, focused, and runs alongside arranging transfer, not before it.

**Focused history**, because it changes urgency and destination: onset and speed of spread, because overnight progression is itself a red flag; difficulty swallowing, breathing, or lying flat, because these are airway symptoms; fluid intake and urine output, because she is diabetic, febrile and barely drinking — dehydration and hyperglycaemia compound each other; her diabetic control, because an HbA1c of ~75 mmol/mol means impaired immune response and poorer tissue penetration; allergies and current medication, because it affects what the hospital gives her.

**Examination — I'd frame it as A-B-C plus the surgical sieve of the swelling**: airway — drooling, raised firm floor of mouth, trismus of 22 mm, and dysphagia are the four findings I say out loud as red flags, because together they suggest infection tracking into the submandibular and sublingual spaces with potential for Ludwig's angina; breathing — respiratory rate 21, rising; circulation — pulse 118 with BP 104/66, a picture consistent with early sepsis. Using a structured tool: on **NEWS2** she scores highly and meets the threshold for urgent escalation; "think sepsis" applies (NICE NG51).

**Dental examination** only to the extent it changes the referral letter: source tooth is the grossly carious lower right six, tender to percussion — I do not need a radiograph today, because imaging must be justified under IRMER 2017 and it would not change my management, which is immediate transfer; definitive imaging (CT) belongs in hospital.

**Working diagnosis:** spreading odontogenic infection of the right submandibular space, crossing toward sublingual/submental spaces, with systemic sepsis, on a background of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. **Differentials** I would name and dismiss quickly: sialadenitis of the submandibular gland, infected cyst, lymphadenitis — but the carious six, the percussion tenderness and the anatomical pattern make the odontogenic source overwhelmingly likely.

domains.name: Management of scenario
domains.model_answer:
Today's safe management is **immediate emergency referral — this patient goes to hospital now, by ambulance**.

My reasoning, said out loud: she has **airway red flags** (trismus 22 mm, dysphagia, drooling, raised floor of mouth), **systemic red flags** (temperature 38.6, pulse 118, RR 21, BP drifting down — a high NEWS2 score), and **host red flags** (poorly controlled diabetes). SDCEP's *Management of Acute Dental Problems* is explicit that swelling with difficulty swallowing, breathing, trismus or systemic upset needs immediate referral to oral and maxillofacial surgery / A&E. Any one of these would tip me; she has all three groups.

Concretely, in the next fifteen minutes I would:

1. **Call 999** and say the words "suspected Ludwig's angina / spreading odontogenic infection with airway compromise and sepsis", because naming the emergency gets the right response priority.
2. **Phone the on-call OMFS registrar** at the receiving unit to hand over directly — SBAR format: situation, background including the diabetes and observations, assessment, and that she is coming by ambulance — because a warm handover prevents her sitting in a waiting room.
3. **Keep her upright**, never supine, because lying her flat can precipitate airway obstruction; keep her calm; nil by mouth from now, because she may need theatre tonight.
4. **Write a referral letter** with observations, timings, medical history, drug history and allergies to travel with her.

What I would **not** do, and why: I would not attempt extraction or incision and drainage in practice, because trismus prevents access, local anaesthetic works poorly in acidotic infected tissue, and she needs airway-protected drainage in theatre. I would not just prescribe oral antibiotics and review Monday — **antibiotics are not a substitute for source control**, and in a septic diabetic patient on a Friday evening that plan risks a fatal deterioration. If transfer were delayed and I were asked about antimicrobials, the decision belongs to the receiving team; hospital treatment will be intravenous — e.g. IV amoxicillin plus metronidazole per local protocol [verify against current BNF/SDCEP and local antimicrobial policy].

domains.name: Management planning & execution
domains.model_answer:
**Stabilise → definitive → maintenance**, being clear about which parts are mine.

**Stabilise (hospital, tonight):** I should be able to describe what I am referring her into, because it justifies the urgency: senior anaesthetic assessment of the airway, possibly awake fibre-optic intubation; IV access, blood cultures, lactate, glucose and ketones — because a septic diabetic can tip into hyperglycaemic emergency; IV fluids and IV antibiotics per the local sepsis pathway ("Sepsis Six" thinking); CT to map the spaces involved; then **theatre for extraction of the source tooth and incision and drainage of the involved spaces** — source control is the definitive emergency treatment. Her diabetes team may need to manage glucose perioperatively.

**Definitive (after discharge, back with me):** she returns with a missing lower right six and, importantly, the same high-caries-risk, poorly controlled diabetic mouth that produced this emergency. My plan: full assessment with appropriate radiographs, now justified under IRMER 2017 because they will change management; stabilise all active caries; remove or restore any other teeth of hopeless prognosis **before** they become the next emergency, because she has demonstrated how badly her host response copes with infection.

**Maintenance:** an intensive prevention plan per *Delivering Better Oral Health* — diet counselling aligned with her diabetic dietary advice, 5,000 ppm fluoride toothpaste [verify against current BNF/SDCEP], short recall intervals per NICE dental recall guidance; and **liaison with her GP and diabetes team with her consent**, because periodontal disease and glycaemic control are bidirectionally linked and her HbA1c of 75 is a shared problem. Replacing the six (implant, bridge, denture, or accept the space — including the 'do nothing' option with its risks of over-eruption and tilting) is a conversation for when she is stable and motivated, with risks and benefits of each option laid out.

**Execution detail examiners like:** I would book her follow-up myself before she leaves the practice pathway, not "tell her to ring us", because patients lost to follow-up after emergencies are the rule, not the exception.

domains.name: Professionalism, ethics & medicolegal
domains.model_answer:
**Consent under pressure:** she is unwell but has capacity — being frightened and febrile does not remove it (Mental Capacity Act 2005: assume capacity, support decision-making). I would explain in plain language what I believe is happening, why hospital is not optional-sounding advice but a potentially life-saving step, and what will likely happen there, because *Montgomery* consent applies just as much in an emergency: she needs the material risks of **not** going — airway obstruction and death — stated clearly and kindly. If she tried to refuse transfer, I would treat that as the highest-stakes informed-refusal conversation of my week: explore why (childcare? fear? cost of missing work?), solve what can be solved, be explicit that this can kill, involve a family member with her agreement, document verbatim, and if she still left, safety-net in writing and alert her GP — and I would be honest that I'd be documenting this thoroughly because the stakes are so high.

**Documentation:** contemporaneous notes with timed observations, my NEWS2/sepsis reasoning, the exact red flags found, who I spoke to at the hospital and when, what was handed over, and copies of the referral letter. In any subsequent scrutiny — and spreading infections that go wrong end up at inquests — the timeline is everything.

**Professional responsibility for the system around me:** this arrived at 4:30 pm Friday; I would stay past closing to complete the handover, because GDC *Standards* principle 1 (put patients' interests first) does not have office hours. I would also reflect on whether she could have been seen earlier in the week — SDCEP acute problem guidance expects practices to triage swelling as urgent — and raise it at a practice meeting or significant-event analysis if our triage failed, because principle 8 requires me to act on things that put patients at risk.

**Duty of candour:** if any part of our handling contributed to the delay, I would be open with her about it, apologise, and record that conversation — being open when things go wrong is both a GDC expectation and the decent thing to do.

**Safety-netting and limits:** my referral threshold in future for her is explicitly lowered — any swelling, straight in. And beyond the point of recognising and referring this emergency, I am clear that her airway, her sepsis and her surgery are for the hospital team; knowing exactly where my role stops is part of managing this safely.

marks_lost: Prescribing oral antibiotics and reviewing after the weekend — the single biggest failure in this scenario; antibiotics are not a substitute for source control.
Attempting extraction or drainage in practice despite trismus and systemic sepsis.
Not naming the airway red flags explicitly (trismus, dysphagia, drooling, raised floor of mouth) or the term Ludwig's angina.
Ignoring the observations — failing to interpret temperature, pulse, RR and BP as sepsis (NEWS2 / NICE NG51).
Missing the significance of poorly controlled diabetes for both severity and future prevention.
Referring by letter alone — no 999 call, no verbal handover to the OMFS team.
Letting her drive herself or sit in a waiting room supine.
No follow-up plan after discharge — the mouth that caused the emergency is still there.

probes.q: She says she'll go to hospital tomorrow morning because she has to collect her children from school. How do you respond?
probes.a: I'd take the concern seriously and solve it practically — can a family member or friend collect the children while she goes now? Then I'd be direct: this infection is spreading toward her airway and overnight it could close it; people die from this, and tonight is the dangerous window. If she still refused I'd document the informed refusal in detail, put safety-netting in writing (immediate 999 if breathing or swallowing worsens), inform her GP, and ask her to ring me — but I would do everything short of coercion to get her in an ambulance today.

probes.q: What is Ludwig's angina and why is it an emergency?
probes.a: Bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces, usually odontogenic. It elevates and displaces the tongue and floor of mouth backwards, causing rapidly progressive airway obstruction — the emergency is the airway, not the infection per se. It needs immediate hospital care: airway secured first, then IV antibiotics and surgical decompression with removal of the source tooth.

probes.q: Why does her diabetes matter here specifically?
probes.a: Three ways: poorly controlled diabetes impairs neutrophil function so infections spread faster and worse; sepsis destabilises glycaemic control, risking hyperglycaemic emergencies — so hospital needs to check glucose and ketones; and long term, her diabetes makes aggressive dental prevention and liaison with her diabetes team essential, because the relationship between oral infection and glycaemic control runs in both directions.

probes.q: If she had presented two days earlier with a localised buccal swelling, no trismus, and normal observations — what changes?
probes.a: That's a localised infection amenable to primary care: local measures are first line — extraction or extirpation of the lower right six with drainage through the tooth or incision of a pointing buccal swelling. Antibiotics only if there is systemic involvement or spreading infection per SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry — e.g. phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days, or amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily [verify against current BNF/SDCEP] — alongside, never instead of, treating the source. Then clear safety-netting: return or A&E immediately if swelling spreads, swallowing or breathing is affected, or she feels systemically unwell.

references: SDCEP — Management of Acute Dental Problems
NICE NG51 — Sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management
NICE NG12 (contrast: this is emergency referral, not a 2-week-wait pathway)
GDC Standards for the Dental Team — principles 1 and 8
